newsitem.title: UK: Globalisation, direct investment leap in 95 - UNCTAD.
newsitem.headline: Globalisation, direct investment leap in 95 - UNCTAD.

text.p: Business globalisation is increasing at a "dramatic" pace and foreign direct investment by trans-national corporations soared in 1995, according to the latest World Investment report from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

Total foreign direct investment (FDI) into developed and developing countries surged by 40 percent in 1995 to reach $315 billion; $100 billion of this went to developing countries, a gain of 15 percent on 1994, the report said.
China alone attracted over $38 billion, and has been the largest developing country recipient since 1992.

Competitive pressures, new technologies, privatisations and national government policies are among some of the factors encouraging record FDI. Regional economic groupings are also stimulating business globalisation, the report said.

U.S. transnational corporations (TNCs) as a group were the largest foreign investors, and the U.S. was the single largest host country for FDI, but Japan now has 19 TNCs in the top 100, up from 11 in 1990.

FDI volume is made up of an estimated 39,000 TNCs with about 270,000 foreign affiliates, which have combined holdings of over $42.7 trillion. The top 100 investors account for about one third of the flows; all are headquartered in developed countries.

The report noted "something new is happening in the dynamics between trade and investment". "Historically, manufacturing firms have traded with foreign enterprises and buyers before directly investing (thus trade preceding international investment). Now the relationship has become more complex."
But if FDI brings economic growth it can also create costs.

"The data shows FDI distribution is uneven. Many developing countries currently obtain very little FDI and are not as yet a significant part of TNC global and regional growth strategies. These countries risk being marginalised," UNCTAD said.

The principal effect of the new environment is that firms are freer to choose how to serve foreign markets -- by producing at home or exporting, by producing in a foreign country for local sale or producing there for export.
"Once a location decision has been made, investment and trade flows are determined simultaneously," the report said.
"The greater inter-twining of FDI and trade...presents new challenges to policy makers, especially as national trade and FDI policies have usually evolved separately," UNCTAD said.

FDI flows are also highly concentrated. The smallest 100 recipient countries received one percent of total investment while the top 10 took 68 percent of total flows. Firms in the U.S., Germany, Britain, Japan and France dominate activity.
Most of the year's FDI can be attributed to huge mergers and acquisitions among developed countries in energy, telecommunications, pharmaceutical and financial services.
UNCTAD lists the biggest TNCs in developed countries as Britain/Netherlands' Royal Dutch Shell with foreign assets of $63.7 billion and total assets of $102 billion in 1994.
Ford of the U.S. is second with $60.6 billion of foreign assets (total $219.4 billion), followed by Exxon with $56.2 billion (total $87.9 billion).

But transnational corporations from developing courntries are becoming more important. Among the top 100, 50 are headquartered in Asia or Latin America, headed by Korea's Daewoo, Hong Kong's Hutchinson Whampoa and Mexico's Cemex.

The report says more information is needed on the forms and types of FDI investment, measures affecting entry and operations of investors and special arrangements like most-favoured-nation status. There are also broader concerns about regulatory controls, investment protection and settlement of disputes.
